newsitem.title: UK: Soaring sterling boosted by UK inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Soaring sterling boosted by UK inflation data.

text.p: Sterling powered above 2.91 German marks to its highest level since May 1991, boosted by stronger-than-expected UK inflation statistics for June.

The pound gained over a pfennig after retail price data showed underlying inflation, excluding mortgage payments, rose 0.3 percent last month. That pushed the annual rate to 2.7 percent from 2.5 percent in May. Economists had expected the rate to stick to 2.5 percent, the government's target.
"This is very supportive of sterling and strengthens the Bank of England's hand for another rate rise this week," said Nick Shamin, currency analyst at ANZ Investment.
The Bank of England trade-weighted index pushed to its highest level since April 1989 at 104.2, up from 103.3 at the close on Monday.
At 0915 GMT the pound was at 2.9700/10 marks and $1.6909/19, compared with 2.9385/95 and $1.6845/55 at the European close on Monday.
Heightened interest rate rise expectations after the data sparked a flurry of buying ahead of the two-day Bank of England monetary committee meeting, starting on Wednesday, traders said.
A surprise drop in manufacturing output in May depressed the pound on Monday as foreign exchange dealers scaled back their rate rise hopes to a quarter point from half a point.

Rate rise expectations have been running wild since last week's budget by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, which was seen as insufficient to restrain Britain's buoyant consumer demand. "The inflation data must get the hawks on the (Bank of England) monetary committee to sound the alarm bells," said a senior trader at a German bank in London. However, economists also pointed to a big increase in seasonal food prices due to exceptionally bad weather in June as the main reason for the strong inflation data. "Elsewhere, the picture was much more benign," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Woody Gundy. "The market's nervousness about the outcome of this week's Bank of England meeting is understandable, but setting interest rates according to the weather might be stretching...things a little too far," he said.
Will sterling now face a sell-the-fact situation if a rate rise is announced on Thursday after the meeting?, traders pondered.
"The market is so geared up for a rate rise that anything less than 50 basis points would be disappointing for sterling," said Shamin.

No change in rates would spark a "blood-bath" for the pound, said Shamin. "It would be sold off all the way to 2.87 marks but that would be a great opportunity to go long again in expectation of a rate rise at a later stage."
